Duplicate of 可, which has a similar sound.
聲也。从二可。古文以爲謌字。

Stacked form of 可 (OC *kʰaːlʔ), perhaps an open mouth with breath going out while talking or singing. In fact, the original meaning of 哥 and perhaps 可 was "to sing; song".
; “elder brother”
: It is a clipping of 阿哥 (MC 'a ka), a borrowing from Xianbei *aqa (“elder brother”) (Mei, 2015). Compare Proto-Mongolic *aka, whence also Mongolian ᠠᠬ᠎ᠠ (ak-a, “elder brother”). Related to 阿干 (MC 'a kan), which is the definite form of the same Xianbei word (Mei, 2015).

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, 《說文解字》 and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The entry for 哥 reads “聲也。从二可。古文以爲謌字” (“sound; formed from two 可; in ancient writing used for 謌”). Duan Yucai says the ‘sound’ gloss is not attested in use in his time and notes that 哥 was then used to call an elder brother. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the earliest graphic formation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「哥」 - Shuowen.org

evidence.source: 漢典, quoting 說文解字 and 說文解字注
evidence.text: The entry for 歌 gives “詠也。从欠哥聲。謌，歌或从言”; its note cites 哥 as “聲也” and says it was used for 謌. This supports 哥 functioning as the phonetic element in 歌 and the historical interchange/use of 哥 for the song word. It does not establish that the stacked 可 graph originally depicted singing or an open mouth; that proposal remains speculative.
evidence.title: 謌 gē - 漢典

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese entry 哥 (citing Zhengzhang 2003 and historical dictionaries)
evidence.text: The entry places 哥 in the 可 phonetic series and reports Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese *kaːl for 哥, 歌, and several other series members, against *kʰaːlʔ for 可. It gives modern Standard Mandarin gē (Hanyu Pinyin) and Guangzhou/Hong Kong Cantonese go1 (Jyutping). Its Qieyun/Guangyun-style entry records 見母, 歌韻, 平聲, 開口一等, fanqie 古俄切; Baxter Middle Chinese ka and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *kaːl are shown. These reconstructions independently support sound relationship while allowing different initials and tones in related series members.
evidence.title: 哥 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: Lin Huayong, 《以「哥」稱父等現象的社會語盲學視野》, Chinese Language Newsletter 80
evidence.text: The article reports that sources before the Northern and Southern dynasties do not show 哥 meaning elder brother, that the kinship sense in written texts appears from the Tang, and cites Tang-era evidence including a Dunhuang vernacular text and imperial usage of 哥 for father. It summarizes competing scholarship connecting kinship 哥 with Xianbei 阿干 and other Altaic-language explanations; these are attributed proposals rather than a settled demonstration of the transmission route.
evidence.title: 以「哥」稱父等現象的社會語盲學視野

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese entry 哥; citation attributed there to Mei 2015
evidence.text: The entry proposes that elder-brother 哥 is a clipping of 阿哥, Middle Chinese 'a ka, borrowed from reconstructed Xianbei *aqa ‘elder brother’; it compares Proto-Mongolic *aka and Mongolian aq-a. This is a secondary assertion. The evidence inspected here did not independently establish the early Xianbei word’s recorded pronunciation or a detailed sound adaptation from *aqa to 阿哥 and then 哥.
evidence.title: 哥 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese entry 哥; historical sources summarized in Lin Huayong
evidence.text: The sources distinguish an older song-related graphic/lexical use from the later kinship sense. The Shuowen account and Han-era textual citations for 哥/歌 support the song association; the kinship use is reported from Tang-era material, with evidence also for ‘father’ and later broader address uses. This evidence does not supply a full dated chain for each extension, nor prove that the kinship word semantically developed from ‘song’; the loan proposal instead treats them as separate word histories sharing a graph.
evidence.title: 以「哥」稱父等現象的社會語盲學視野

evidence.text: The entry’s cited epigraphic sample for 謌 is from the late Spring and Autumn period (余贎乘兒鐘, 集成 186); it also lists Chu manuscripts, Qin manuscripts, and Shuowen seal forms. Since these are forms of 謌, not necessarily standalone 哥, they show the song graph’s development and the哥 phonetic component in an early compound, but do not by themselves establish the chronology of standalone 哥’s shapes. No glyph image was visually assessed in this research.
evidence.title: 謌 gē - 漢典

evidence.text: The entry records Standard Mandarin gē (Pinyin), Guangzhou/Hong Kong Cantonese go1 (Jyutping), Japanese Go-on and Kan-on ka, Tō-on ko, and Korean reading ka. These readings belong to distinct languages and traditions; they do not prove the character’s origin or the Xianbei etymology.
evidence.title: 哥 - Wiktionary

evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry says 哥 means “sound,” is formed “from two 可,” and in ancient writing was used for 謌. Duan Yucai’s later note says he did not find the ‘sound’ sense in use in his time, says people then called an elder brother 哥, and reports Han-dynasty use of 哥 for 歌. This is a historical dictionary account, not independent proof of the earliest form or the referent of 可.
evidence.title: 說文解字「哥」 - Shuowen.org

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, 哥 entry
evidence.text: This compiled entry repeats the Shuowen analysis and cites the transmitted Song shu statement that a Former Han figure ‘was good at singing.’ It also quotes Bai Juyi’s ninth-century “祭浮梁大兄” for elder-brother usage and a later text for broader male address. These references show song and kinship uses represented by 哥, but do not date the creation of its stacked form or establish that one word meaning developed from the other.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, 歌 entry
evidence.text: The entry describes late Spring and Autumn bronze song graphs written 訶, analyzed as 言 plus sound element 可; it cites a Chu bronze inscription with a phrase glossed ‘eat and sing and dance.’ It also reports that 可 and 哥 both served as sound elements in the 歌 series and cites the Shuowen analysis 歌 ‘from 欠, with 哥 as sound.’ The dated bronze examples are song-related graphs, not securely attested standalone 哥 forms.
evidence.record_character: 歌 / 哥 (related graph; relation explicitly scoped)
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, 可 entry
evidence.text: This entry describes early 可 as containing 口 and 丂, while stating that the initial graph’s meaning is unsettled and listing competing interpretations of 丂. It reports that 可 was later borrowed for ‘can/may’ and labels the theory that 可 itself was an old graph for 歌 as unconfirmed, noting no bronze use of 可 for 歌 in its account. This uncertainty about the original referent does not remove the separate evidence for 可’s sound role in later song compounds.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese 哥 entry, reporting Zhengzhang (2003)
evidence.text: In the Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstruction system, the entry gives 哥 *kaːl and 可 *kʰaːlʔ. The shared rhyme with differing initial and tone supports a historical sound relationship, rather than exact identity of pronunciation. The entry also gives Standard Mandarin gē (Hanyu Pinyin) and Guangzhou/Hong Kong Cantonese go1 (Jyutping); these modern readings are language-specific and do not establish origin.
evidence.title: 哥 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, 哥 entry
evidence.text: The entry gives the Guangyun fanqie 古俄切 and categories 見母, 歌韻, 平聲, 開口一等 for 哥. This is a traditional rhyme-book record, distinct from modern Mandarin and from the Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstruction.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: Alexander Vovin and David McCraw, “Old Turkic Kinship Terms in Early Middle Chinese”
evidence.text: The authors argue that early Tang kinship terms such as 哥 kâ are difficult to document securely before the Tang; they note uncertainty over the date of the Mulan ballad. They report fifth-century Chinese transcription 啊干 for a Xianbei elder-brother term in Song shu 96, reconstructed by them as Early Middle Chinese ʔa-kan, and argue that 哥 cannot be a direct loan from this form because its final -n does not match. They propose an indirect path through Old Turkic aqa, while acknowledging that the Turkic form’s late attestation remains unexplained. This is a scholarly proposal, not a settled route; the Chinese transcription and its reconstructed reading do not independently recover the native Xianbei pronunciation.
evidence.title: Old Turkic Kinship Terms in Early Middle Chinese

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese 哥 entry, attributing proposal to Mei 2015
evidence.text: The entry proposes that kinship 哥 is clipped from 阿哥, reconstructed there as Middle Chinese 'a ka, and borrowed from Xianbei *aqa ‘elder brother’; it compares Proto-Mongolic *aka and Mongolian aq-a. This differs from Vovin and McCraw’s proposed Turkic-mediated route. The sources inspected do not independently establish the pronunciation of the Xianbei source word or every transmission step.
evidence.title: 哥 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: Alexander Vovin and David McCraw, “Old Turkic Kinship Terms in Early Middle Chinese”
evidence.text: The authors characterize several new kinship terms as appearing in early Tang texts and say pre-Tang evidence is hard to establish; they treat the Mulan ballad’s date as uncertain. Their bibliography dates some cited works or compilations separately, including Song shu’s first redaction before 557 and ninth-century Bai Juyi material. Therefore a text’s compilation date, a narrated event’s date, and the date of a word’s use should not be conflated. The inspected evidence does not provide a complete dated chain for later extensions such as honorific address or regional parent terms.
evidence.title: Old Turkic Kinship Terms in Early Middle Chinese

evidence.text: The 謌 entry lists a late Spring and Autumn bronze inscription example from 余贎乘兒鐘 (集成 186), along with Chu manuscripts, Qin manuscripts, and Shuowen seal forms. These attest forms of 謌/song-related writing and its phonetic component, not necessarily standalone 哥. The page does not establish a continuous graphic sequence from those forms to modern 哥.
evidence.record_character: 謌 / 哥 (related graph; relation explicitly scoped)
evidence.title: 謌 gē - 漢典

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》, 哥 entry
evidence.text: The dictionary presents the Shuowen analysis and song gloss, then lists elder-brother and same-generation male address senses. Its cited received graph form is Shuowen seal script; the displayed reference section marks several oracle, bronze, and manuscript form resources as not publicly viewable there. This inspected page does not independently furnish a sequence of dated standalone 哥 forms.
evidence.title: [A00587] 哥 - 教育部《異體字字典》

It is a modern redraw of an ancient-script form, not an artifact photograph. The page reports CC0/public-domain reuse for the picture.

It was made with Inkscape and is a modern redraw, not an ancient artifact photograph. Commons states public-domain reuse and records the original permission as courtesy from the Sears site.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

search_audit.query: 漢語多功能字庫 哥 可 歌 sound role Guangyun readings early bronze song graph
search_audit.outcome: Inspected entries for 哥, 可, 歌, and Taiwan Ministry of Education variant dictionary. Found early song compound evidence for 可 as a sound element, an explicit caveat on 可’s initial graph interpretation, Guangyun categories, and no publicly viewable standalone early 哥 form sequence on the inspected reference page.

gaps: The inspected sources did not provide a reliable sequence of dated standalone 哥 glyph forms from oracle bone through bronze, seal, clerical, and regular scripts. The late Spring and Autumn bronze example located is 謌, not clearly standalone 哥; no glyph image was visually inspected.

The explanation that duplicated 可 depicts a mouth with breath or that 哥/可 originally meant ‘sing/song’ is speculative in the consulted secondary entry. Shuowen records a sound gloss, a two-可 analysis, and use for 謌, but does not explain the depicted referent of 可.

The proposed Xianbei *aqa source is reconstructed and secondarily cited. The consulted material did not independently verify primary documentation of the source-language form, its recoverable pronunciation, or each borrowing/adaptation step into 阿哥 and clipped 哥.

Available accounts report Tang-era attestations and older song-related usage, but do not establish a complete chronology for all semantic extensions such as ‘elder brother,’ ‘father,’ and generalized honorific/address uses. The graph’s reuse for kinship does not prove a semantic development from song.

A distinction between the sound component 可 inside 哥 and whole-graph use of 哥 for song must be maintained: the 可-to-哥 sound relationship is supported by series reconstruction; the Xianbei hypothesis concerns the borrowed kinship word represented by 哥, not the phonetic role of 可.
The evidence inspected does not establish a component origin_form distinct from 可 for the 可 element. No independent graphic ancestor or corruption account for the stacked shape was verified.

No reliable continuous sequence of dated standalone 哥 forms from oracle bone through bronze, seal, clerical, and regular scripts was established. The located early bronze song forms are 訶/謌, not securely standalone 哥.

The duplicated-可 shape has a Shuowen explanation but its earliest graphic origin and any corruption or replacement history remain unverified. A mouth-and-breath depiction or singing-origin account is speculative in the inspected material.

The evidence supports 可 as a sound element in song-related compounds and 哥 as historically used for song; it does not demonstrate that the kinship word developed semantically from ‘song.’ The kinship word’s proposed borrowing route is disputed.

The source Xianbei word’s exact native pronunciation is not independently recoverable from the inspected evidence. The Chinese transcription 啊干 and its Early Middle Chinese reconstruction ʔa-kan are not proof of the separately proposed Xianbei *aqa pronunciation; the direct and Turkic-mediated accounts differ.

The sources provide some dated or date-bounded song and kinship references but do not establish a complete chronology for elder-brother use, father address, generalized address, and dialectal extensions. Compilation dates and dates of narrated events must be kept distinct.

Only modern redrawings of 可 were established as reusable visual candidates. They are component examples, not images of standalone 哥 and not artifact photographs. No pixel-level visual inspection was performed in this research. The attempted Xiaoxuetang individual record was not accessible through the inspected page response.

limitations.text: Both images depict 可, not 哥, and are modern redrawings rather than photographs of ancient artifacts. The evidence does not establish a reliable dated sequence of standalone 哥 forms or the earliest origin of its stacked shape.

Shuowen analyzes 哥 as formed from two 可 and records its use for 謌, but this does not establish what the earliest form depicted. A mouth-and-breath or singing-origin interpretation for the stacked shape remains speculative.
